cards.title: Introduction to Streams
cards.content:
The Concept of Streams

In Java, I/O operations are performed using Streams. A stream represents a continuous flow of data from a source (input) to a destination (output).

Streams are classified into two main categories based on the data type they handle:

  • Byte Streams: Handle 8-bit raw bytes (e.g., images, audio, binary data). Principal classes: InputStream and OutputStream.
  • Character Streams: Handle 16-bit Unicode characters (text files). Principal classes: Reader and Writer.

cards.title: Reading Files with Byte Streams
cards.content:
Using FileInputStream

To read raw binary data, we use the FileInputStream class. It reads the file byte by byte. When the end of the file is reached, the read() method returns -1.

FileInputStream in = null;
try {
    in = new FileInputStream('input.dat');
    int data;
    while ((data = in.read()) != -1) {
        // process byte
    }
} finally {
    if (in != null) in.close();
}

cards.title: Character Streams & Buffering
cards.content:
Efficient Text I/O with Buffering

Reading directly from disk can be highly inefficient. Wrapping a FileReader in a BufferedReader creates an internal memory buffer. Instead of calling the OS for every single character, chunks of characters are loaded into memory at once.

BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new FileReader('notes.txt'));
String line;
while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
    System.out.println(line);
}

Note: readLine() returns null when the end of the character stream is reached.

cards.title: Automatic Resource Management
cards.content:
Try-With-Resources

Prior to Java 7, streams had to be explicitly closed inside a finally block, risking leaks or nested exceptions. Java 7 introduced try-with-resources, which automatically closes any class implementing AutoCloseable at the end of the statement block.

try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader('data.txt'))) {
    System.out.println(br.readLine());
} catch (IOException e) {
    e.printStackTrace();
}
// BufferedReader is automatically closed here

cards.title: Java NIO.2 (Non-blocking I/O)
cards.content:
Introduction to NIO.2

Java 7 introduced NIO.2 (new package: java.nio.file) as a modern replacement for legacy java.io.File capabilities. Key abstractions include:

  • Path: Replaces java.io.File and represents locating files system-agnostically.
  • Paths: Helper utility class containing static methods returning a Path object.
  • Files: Utility class packed with static operations such as Files.readAllLines(path) or Files.write(path, bytes).

cards.title: Object Serialization in Java
cards.content:
Writing Objects to Disk

Java allows converting an object state into a byte stream via Serialization. Objects must implement the marker interface java.io.Serializable to be eligible.

Use the transient keyword on fields you do not want to be serialized (e.g., passwords, temp tokens, or database connection instances).

public class User implements Serializable {
    private String username;
    private transient String password; // Will not be saved
}
